detail: Claim text is correct and the simplified flag is appropriate, but the fuller_truth is mechanistically thin. It lists thrombomodulin as a platelet 'protection'. Thrombomodulin acts indirectly: it binds thrombin, which takes away a strong platelet agonist and switches on protein C. It also leaves out the two other main endothelial antiplatelet mechanisms: nitric oxide and CD39 (ecto-ADPase, which breaks down ADP). Nothing here is false; it is just incomplete.
correction: fuller_truth: 'Intact endothelium also releases nitric oxide, breaks down ADP on its surface (CD39), and carries thrombomodulin, which binds thrombin so less thrombin is available to activate platelets. Prostacyclin is one of several brakes.'
correction_source: None of the current sources covers NO or CD39. A source needs to be found (e.g., a PMC endothelium/platelet review) before this text is added.

detail: The claim lists four triggers (collagen, ADP, thrombin, TXA2). Only sp-txa2 supports the full list. The OpenStax passage supports collagen exposure and platelet clumping only, so ADP, thrombin and TXA2 rest on one source. The physiology itself is correct.
correction: Add a second passage naming the soluble agonists.
correction_source: pmc-vwf-platelets: "In this model, thrombus formation involves the release of soluble platelet agonists such as ADP and thromboxane A 2 (TXA 2 ) and the activation of the αIIbβ3 integrin, the receptor for fibrinogen and VWF" (verified in pmc-vwf-platelets.txt). Thrombin still needs a second source.

The duration ('up to about 30 minutes, can last hours') is supported only by OpenStax. The sp-hemostasis passage ('Within about 30 minutes of damage... vascular spasm ensues') is about onset, not duration, and it is itself misleading: vascular spasm starts immediately, not within a 30-minute delay. The claim relies on a passage that is wrong for this purpose. The same passage is also used in c-plt-4.
correction: Remove the sp-hemostasis passage and find a second source that states the duration of vascular spasm.

The claim text is correct and the pmc-vwf-platelets passage (verified) supports it: the A1 site is exposed under arterial shear, and there is no binding in static conditions. The sp-vwf passage is mechanistically wrong for this use. It says vWF multimers 'unfold at the A2 domain' and so expose platelet-binding sites. Unfolding of A2 exposes the ADAMTS13 cleavage site; the GPIb-binding site is in A1. Only one passage is valid.
correction: Drop the sp-vwf passage or trim it to the shear-unfolding/anchoring part without the A2 attribution, and add a second source for the A1 shear exposure.

detail: This is true but incomplete, and it is NOT flagged as simplified. The claim and edge e4 present GPIb–vWF binding as the platelet activator. In fact GPIb–vWF mainly tethers platelets under high shear and sends only a weak activating signal. Firm adhesion and strong activation at the wound come from the collagen receptors GPVI and α2β1, which do not appear anywhere in the module. A learner would conclude that collagen acts only through vWF.
correction: Add simplified: {what: 'GPIb is shown as the adhesion receptor that activates the platelet.', fuller_truth: 'Under high shear, GPIb-vWF is the first grip (tethering). Platelets also bind collagen directly through GPVI and α2β1; GPVI-collagen is a major activation signal, and those receptors are needed for stable adhesion.'}
correction_source: pmc-vwf-platelets: "Under high shear, it was clearly established that the VWF/GPIb-IX-V interaction is the predominant receptor-ligand interaction initiating platelet adhesion. For stable adhesion, the collagen receptors (GPVI and α2β1 integrin) as well as the fibronectin receptor (α5β1 integrin) are required." (verified)

correction: Trim the passage so it does not use 'initiate platelet aggregation', or replace it.

detail: The claim text is correct (ADP and TXA2). The sp-histology-platelets passage, however, says activated platelets 'release... thrombin'. That is wrong: platelets do not store or release thrombin; thrombin is generated on the activated platelet surface by prothrombinase. The claim leans on a passage containing an error. sp-platelet-activation is fine. The same passage appears in c-adp-2 and c-txa2-1.

detail: Minor. The claim text ('switches on GPIIb/IIIa') is correct. The sp-platelet-activation passage says ADP is 'inducing the expression of the GPIIb/IIIa receptor', which suggests the receptor is absent on resting platelets. GPIIb/IIIa is already present; ADP mainly converts it to its high-affinity active form by inside-out signaling. Also, P2Y1 starts the response (shape change, weak aggregation) while P2Y12 sustains and amplifies it. The '(and P2Y1)' wording is acceptable.
correction: Add or substitute the sp-txa2 inside-out passage so the cited mechanism is activation, not expression.
correction_source: sp-txa2: "This intracellular signaling pathway results in a conformational change of GP IIb/IIIa to an active form and is referred to as 'inside-out' signaling."

The passage, edge e6 and m1-q07 variant 2 together imply the bridge comes from granules. 'Clotting factors circulate as zymogens and are activated into enzymes' over-generalizes. It is false for factors V and VIII, which are procofactors activated to non-enzyme cofactors. It is also false for fibrinogen (a structural substrate) and for tissue factor (a membrane cofactor). It contradicts the module's own cofactor entry ('helpers, not enzymes themselves'). It is not flagged as simplified. The sp-coag-pathways passage makes the same over-generalization. The why_here line has the same problem: 'Clotting factors travel in the blood as zymogens'.
correction: 'Most clotting factors (the serine proteases II, VII, IX, X, XI, XII) circulate as zymogens and are activated into enzymes. Factors V and VIII circulate as inactive cofactors, and fibrinogen is the substrate turned into fibrin.' Fix why_here to match.
correction_source: sp-hemostasis: "Activated factor IX (factor IXa) binds with its cofactor – activated factor VIII (factor VIIIa)..."; sp-coag-pathways: "factor Xa requires factor V as a cofactor"; openstax-hemostasis: "thrombin converts factor I, the soluble fibrinogen, into the insoluble fibrin protein strands" (verified)
